facts.label: Task suite
facts.note: Counting, evidence reading, supported conclusions, and two combined research tasks.

facts.label: Repetitions
facts.note: 32 runs, $2.65. The final study runs 3 repetitions of 11 tasks.

facts.label: Grading
facts.note: Runtime checks never see the key. Programmatic for counts, human review for labels.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.note: Pass rate, cost per successful answer, and time from acceptance to a terminal state.

test.headline: 8 tasks × 4 combinations
test.body: One run each — 32 runs, $2.65 in total. Every answer is graded offline against a private key the agent never sees.

findings.headline: The cost gap is real. The quality ranking is not.
findings.intro: Each bar is a measured value with its 95% interval. Where two intervals overlap, the order of the bars is not a finding — read only the separations.
findings.time_to_result: Medians 20–36 s, 90th percentiles 39–102 s, against deadlines of 300–400 s. **No configuration missed a deadline.** Time did not discriminate here, so it is reported and set aside.

cost.note: **C ends at $0.048; B and D begin near $0.11.** No overlap — this is the study's one solid separation. A's interval overlaps both Opus configurations, so A cannot be ranked against them at all.

quality.note: **Every interval reaches 100%, and A's reaches down to 25%.** C passed all eight, so every resample returns 100% — a ceiling with no failures in it, not precision. Across all five pairwise comparisons the interval contains zero.

rows.question: Can better tools make the cheaper model the more economical qualifying option?
What does choosing Opus buy with baseline tools?
Is Opus worth its cost once tools are redesigned?
Does the redesign improve Opus too?

contrasts.note: “Suggestive” means the point estimate favours one side but the interval includes zero. “Inconclusive” means neither side is favoured. Nothing here reaches “supported”.

recommendation.headline: If you had to choose today, choose C — and keep testing.
paragraphs: Haiku with the redesigned tools answered every task it was given and cost less per successful answer than either Opus configuration, with no overlap in the intervals. On cost, that is a genuine result.

The reason to keep testing is that its **quality** advantage is not established. At eight tasks nothing is separated on quality, two of C's eight grades are still with a second reviewer, and the 80% floor it clears is a placeholder. The honest label for this recommendation is **suggestive**.

settle_it.text: Run the full 132: 11 tasks × 4 combinations × 3 repetitions, instead of 8 tasks once.
Freeze the quality floor, time rule and confidence criteria before those runs, not after.
Finish the seven grades still awaiting a second reviewer — two of them are C's.
Measure the three redesigned features separately, since they shipped together here.

caveats.heading: Four things this evidence cannot tell you

items.title: Whether a passing run is correct
items.body: Runtime checks catch malformed answers, invented quotes, unfinished pagination and wrong subtraction. They cannot judge whether the evidence supports the claim. One run here passed every check and was still wrong by one opening.

items.title: How these models rank in general
items.body: This is a case study on one task suite over one frozen archive, chosen to be diagnostic rather than representative. It is not a model ranking, and the two models differ in more than size.

items.title: What the job market did
items.body: A collection window holds postings first captured in that range. Counts describe what the pipeline captured — never every job that was open, and never hiring demand.

items.title: That these results are final
items.body: These are labelled development runs used to calibrate validators and settings. The 132-run evaluation has not started, and results stay provisional until grading and costs are complete.

try.cta: Pick one of the three questions and see how all four combinations answered it — including the run that passed every check and was still wrong.
try.intro: Three real questions from the archive. Each was given to all four combinations and graded against a verified answer. Pick one to see how they compare.
try.best_rule: Best = the cheapest combination that answered correctly.
try.ranking_note: One graded run per combination is not a success rate, and one question is not the suite — the suite-wide comparison is on the Findings tab.

questions.short: How many distinct openings did Anthropic actually have in August?
questions.why: 13 records collapse into 9 openings. The identity rule decides the answer.
questions.task: In collection window pai-2026-08, how many raw posting records are there for Anthropic and how many distinct openings do they represent under the published identity rule? List each group of records that collapse into one opening, with the record IDs and sources involved, and explain why the raw and distinct counts differ.
questions.best_why: Every combination got this right, so the only thing separating them is price — and A did it for $0.017, a tenth of what Opus charged.
questions.best_caveat: This is the easy end of the suite: one page of records and a published rule to apply. A handled it here, but A failed three of the eight tasks overall. Cheapest-that-worked on one question is not the same as reliable.

A.note: Correct — and the cheapest run in the whole matrix.

repetitions.summary: Anthropic has 13 raw posting records in pai-2026-08 representing 9 distinct openings. The counts differ because 4 records collapse into 2 openings: 3 records for “Product Manager, Cyber Security” and 3 for “Product Manager, Business Technology”, both spanning greenhouse and jsearch.

B.note: Correct, with the fullest account of why the counts differ.

repetitions.summary: 13 raw records collapse into 9 distinct openings. Two title groups contain multiple records: “product manager, cyber security” (1 greenhouse + 2 jsearch) and “product manager, business technology” (2 greenhouse, for US and London, + 1 jsearch). The gap of 4 arises from the same opening captured by more than one source, duplicated within jsearch, or listed under two locations — plus a trailing space in one greenhouse title removed by trimming.

C.note: Correct, reached through the counts mode rather than tallying by hand.

repetitions.summary: In pai-2026-08, Anthropic has 13 raw posting records representing 9 distinct openings. Two titles appear in multiple raw records across sources: “Product Manager, Cyber Security” (1 greenhouse + 2 jsearch) and “Product Manager, Business Technology” (2 greenhouse + 1 jsearch). The remaining 7 openings appear once each.

D.note: Correct, and it names the trailing-space title variant explicitly.

repetitions.summary: raw_count = 13 collapsing to distinct_count = 9. Two title groups absorb the extra records: “Product Manager, Cyber Security” (1 greenhouse with a trailing space in the title, 2 identical jsearch records) and “Product Manager, Business Technology” (2 greenhouse records for different locations plus 1 jsearch). The gap of 4 is entirely cross-source and cross-location duplication of the same (company, title) pair.

questions.short: For these four postings, is agent experience required, preferred, or just mentioned?
questions.why: One role is built entirely around agents yet asks nothing of the candidate.
questions.task: For each of four postings in collection window pai-2026-05, classify whether experience with AI agents is required of candidates, preferred, or only mentioned without being a candidate qualification. Give one label per posting with a verbatim supporting quote.
questions.best_why: C returned all four labels correctly for $0.020 — less than the run that failed outright, and a fifth of either Opus configuration.
questions.best_caveat: A never produced a valid answer here at all: its submission stayed malformed through the one repair. The labels it was trying to submit also called OpenAI's agent-heavy role a requirement — the exact trap this task is built on.

A.note: No valid answer: the submission stayed malformed after its one repair.

repetitions.summary: No answer was returned — summary is null and the run ended incomplete on a persistent structure failure. The labels in its rejected attempts called both Lovable's and OpenAI's roles “required”, where the key says OpenAI's is only mentioned.

B.note: All four labels correct, each tied to the heading that settles it.

repetitions.summary: Only Lovable's “Product Manager (Agents)” makes agent experience an explicit candidate qualification, so it is required. Adobe's places agentic-AI knowledge in its “Preferred” block. Stripe's mentions AI agents only in the team narrative. OpenAI's “Product Manager, API Agents” is entirely about agentic products, but its candidate list names PM tenure, developer-product experience, ambiguity and collaboration — no agent qualification — so agents are job scope, not a requirement.

C.note: All four labels correct, at a fifth of Opus's price.

repetitions.summary: Lovable's Product Manager (Agents) explicitly requires hands-on experience building and shipping agent-based systems. Adobe's Product Manager – Adobe Target lists agentic AI concepts only as a preferred qualification. Stripe's Product Manager, Link Consumer Product mentions AI agents as market context but does not list agent experience as a qualification. OpenAI's Product Manager, API Agents centres on agent infrastructure but does not require or prefer prior agent experience.

D.note: All four correct, with the fullest quotation of the qualification lists.

repetitions.summary: Reading all four full descriptions: Lovable's makes hands-on agent-building an explicit requirement; Adobe's lists agentic-AI knowledge only under “Preferred”; Stripe's mentions agents only when describing the team's market context; and OpenAI's asks for PM tenure, developer-product track record, API design intuition and collaboration — not agent experience — so agents appear as job scope rather than a stated candidate qualification.

questions.short: Fewer postings were captured in the later week. Does that show hiring fell?
questions.why: There is a real collection gap. The honest answer is no — and it has to say why.
questions.task: Compare collection windows pai-w-2026-08-10 (S1) and pai-w-2026-08-24 (S2). For PM postings whose title or description contains the literal term 'agent', report the number of distinct openings captured in each window under the published identity rule, and state whether the data establishes that fewer such openings were posted in the S2 week.
questions.best_why: C got both counts and the coverage gap right for $0.076 — roughly a quarter of what either Opus configuration charged for the same conclusion.
questions.best_caveat: A is the cautionary case on this page: it passed every runtime check and was still wrong, reporting 23 openings where the key says 24. Only offline grading against the private key caught it. Open both runs and compare.

A.note: Passed every check and was still wrong: 23 openings where the key says 24.

repetitions.summary: Comparing PM postings with 'agent' in the title or description between pai-w-2026-08-10 (S1) and pai-w-2026-08-24 (S2), the data shows 38 distinct openings in S1 and 23 distinct openings in S2, a decline of 15. However, the data does not establish that fewer such openings were posted in the S2 week, because S2 has partial coverage: jsearch reported zero records for 5 of 7 days, and greenhouse had partial fetches on 4 days.

B.note: Correct, and correctly refuses to call the drop a decline.

repetitions.summary: s1_distinct = 38 (from 49 raw records) and s2_distinct = 24 (from 33 raw), an absolute change of −14. The data does NOT establish that fewer openings were posted in the S2 week: S2 coverage is partial — jsearch returned 0 records on 5 of 7 days despite an OK status, and one greenhouse board failed with 404 on 4 days — while S1 coverage is complete on all three sources. decline_established = false.

C.note: Correct on both counts and on the coverage gap, for a quarter of Opus's cost.

repetitions.summary: Under the published identity rule, S1 (pai-w-2026-08-10) captured 38 distinct openings while S2 (pai-w-2026-08-24) captured 24, a decline of 14. However, S2 experienced partial coverage — jsearch had 5 zero-record days and greenhouse had 4 partial days due to board failures — while S1 had complete coverage. This prevents establishing that fewer openings were actually posted; it only shows fewer were captured.

D.note: Correct, same conclusion as B at a similar price.

repetitions.summary: s1_distinct = 38 (49 raw records) and s2_distinct = 24 (33 raw), an absolute change of −14. This does NOT establish that fewer openings were posted in S2: jsearch returned zero records on 5 of 7 days and greenhouse was partial on 4 days, while S1 was complete on all three sources for all 7 days. The captured-count gap is confounded by collection gaps, so decline_established = false.

review.title: Graded WRONG offline — no check caught it
review.body: The private key gives S2 = 24 distinct openings and a change of −14. This run said 23 and −15. Every runtime check passed: the structure was repaired, the references were real, the subtraction was internally consistent. Miscounting distinct pairs is invisible to the runtime.
